extraction.name: XTREME-S
extraction.description: A benchmark for evaluating universal cross-lingual speech representations covering 102 languages from 10+ language families across four task families: speech recognition, classification, speech-to-text translation and retrieval, spanning 3 different domains.
extraction.creator: Alexis Conneau, Ankur Bapna, Yu Zhang, Min Ma, Patrick von Platen, Anton Lozhkov, Colin Cherry, Ye Jia, Clara Rivera, Mihir Kale, Daan Van Esch, Vera Axelrod, Simran Khanuja, Jonathan H. Clark, Orhan Firat, Michael Auli, Sebastian Ruder, Jason Riesa, Melvin Johnson
extraction.rai:dataCollection: XTREME-S is a benchmark that aggregates existing multilingual speech datasets covering 102 languages from 10+ language families across 3 different domains and 4 task families (speech recognition, classification, speech-to-text translation and retrieval). The benchmark includes datasets like Fleurs, MLS (Multilingual LibriSpeech), and VoxPopuli.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The benchmark uses existing speech datasets including Fleurs, MLS (Multilingual LibriSpeech), and VoxPopuli, which contain unlabeled speech data across multiple languages. The raw data consists of speech recordings from various domains with different amounts of data per language, with Western European languages having larger amounts of unlabeled data compared to other language groups.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For Fleurs dataset: collected between one and three recordings for each sentence (2.3 on average), with speakers of train sets different than speakers from dev/test sets. For Minds-14: merged monolingual datasets into a single multilingual dataset with 30-20-50% train-dev-test split.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Between one and three recordings per sentence (average 2.3) for Fleurs dataset
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The benchmark shows performance disparities across geographical language groups, with Western European languages achieving better results (11.5 average WER) compared to Sub-Saharan African (26.7 average WER) or South Asian (20.7) languages, partly due to larger amounts of unlabeled data available for Western European languages from MLS and VoxPopuli.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark has significant performance gaps between language families and geographical groups. Reducing these gaps across geographical groups is identified as an important research direction for future work.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark aims to make speech technology available in all languages to give speakers of under-represented languages an equal voice on the Internet and the possibility to make their content and culture known outside of their language cluster. It enables rapid access to data-efficient speech technology for all the world's languages.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The benchmark covers 102 languages spanning more than 10 language families, from high-resource to low-resource languages with different scripts, representing diverse geographical groups including Western European, Sub-Saharan African, and South Asian language groups.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The benchmark is designed for evaluation of multilingual speech representation learning through fine-tuning on downstream tasks. It covers four task families: recognition, translation, classification and retrieval. Guidelines specify that at fine-tuning time, submissions should leverage only the ASR supervision of each task, with specific rules for using external supervision and language models. The benchmark is meant for training, testing, and validation across various data regimes from a few hours to more than a thousand hours of supervision.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Test sets are available in open-source and publicly accessible. All tasks are directly open-sourced and made easily accessible. Results are double-checked through submission of model predictions for each task. The benchmark encourages reproducibility and requires that extra supervision and unlabeled data be easily accessible by other teams, with the exception of exploration of very large-scale speech pre-training using proprietary data.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: TTS-augmented data can be used for pre-training and augmentation. Additional unlabeled speech data can be used for pre-training and self-training. Multi-task learning across datasets is allowed. For speech translation, text-to-text machine translation data from sources like Opus can be used with TTS systems to augment training sets.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Smart filtering methods can be applied to unlabeled text datasets (mC4 and Wikipedia) to adapt them to particular tasks and domains. Language model decoding is allowed with explicit reporting requirements.

name.evidence: We introduce XTREME-S, a new benchmark to evaluate universal cross-lingual speech representations in many languages.

description.evidence: XTREME-S covers four task families: speech recognition, classification, speech-to-text translation and retrieval. Covering 102 languages from 10+ language families, 3 different domains and 4 task families, XTREME-S aims to simplify multilingual speech representation evaluation

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: XTREME-S covers 102 languages with various language families, from high-resource to low-resource, and different scripts... results are much better on the Western European group (with 11.5 average WER) than on other groups like Sub-Saharan African (26.7 average WER) or South Asian (20.7)

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: At ﬁne-tuning time, we ask that submissions leverage only the ASR supervision of each task... Tasks cover several domains and data regimes, from a few hours of supervision to more than a thousand hours... The goal of the benchmark is not to prove that using more supervision leads to better performance but to discover new speech methods that lead to better data-efﬁcient performance, in many languages.

rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan.evidence: Test sets are available in open-source and are not hidden to the public... Tasks cover several domains and data regimes, from a few hours of supervision to more than a thousand hours, and are all directly open-sourced and made easily accessible... In the exception of the exploration of very large-scale speech pre-training using proprietary data, which is encouraged and may be considered as a separate track, all extra supervision as well as unlabeled data should be easily accessible by other teams.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: Additional unlabeled speech data can be used for pre-training but also for self-training and other methods... We do encourage submissions that also use different unlabeled speech, although preferably only in the case where there is a substantial difference (e.g. much smaller or much larger, or from more diverse sources, or using TTS-augmented data etc)... For speech translation, additional supervision can be used in the form of open-sourced text-to-text machine translation data (e.g. from Opus) but any such data should be detailed explicitly in the submission and paper for clear comparisons to other methods. The TTS systems used to potentially augment the training set from the MT data should be reproducible.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: We hope the community can also develop smarter ways to adapt these very large unlabeled text datasets to each particular task and domain through filtering methods... When doing smart filtering of unlabeled text data, the technique should be explained clearly and the data released in open-source when possible.
